title: Checkout slows to a halt
summary: Draft investigation of slow queries and database connection pressure. The workload and worker-scaling trap require validation before publication.
publicationBlockers: Define the worker class, request concurrency, connection lifetime, job-worker demand, and database budget. Pool capacity alone does not establish connection exhaustion.
Measure the missing-index fault, reference fix, and worker-scaling trap. Confirm the actual error type and update the alert, evidence, and debrief before publication.
learningObjectives: Relate application worker and pool settings to the database connection limit.
Distinguish a capacity symptom from the slow query that causes it.
Predict how adding workers affects other clients of a shared database.

provenance.notes: Draft written to prove the environment contract. The pool exhaustion pattern is common, but this version is not adapted from a specific incident report.

journeys.label: Browse order history and check out

alert.title: Checkout latency p95 above 2 seconds
alert.summary: Checkout latency has risen and some requests time out. Investigate query time, worker capacity, and actual database connection use.

healthProbes.publicLabel: Background job worker lost its database connection

plantedFault.summary: Proposed fault: orders.customer_id has no index, so order-history queries scan the table. Four pools with size 10 and overflow 10 permit at most 80 connections, but open them only on demand. The worker model and workload needed to produce connection pressure have not been established.

referenceFix.description: Proposed fix: create the missing index without blocking writes, then measure query latency and request recovery. Idle pooled connections can remain open after load falls.
commands: psql -U postgres -d shop -c 'CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS orders_customer_id_idx ON orders (customer_id);'

traps.description: Proposed trap to validate: more workers increase actual concurrent database demand until the job worker cannot acquire a connection. Larger configured pool capacity alone is not sufficient to cause this failure.

hints.text: Check how many database connections are open and what they are waiting on, for example in pg_stat_activity.
Look at the query plan for the slowest request path before changing capacity.

debrief.rootCause: Proposed root cause: a missing index on orders.customer_id makes the order-history query scan the table and hold connections longer. Whether requests wait for workers, pool checkouts, or database admission depends on the workload. This draft needs measurements before those symptoms can be attributed.
causalChain: The order history query has no usable index and scans the orders table.
Each slow query holds a pooled connection for longer.
Measure whether the observed limit is worker concurrency, pool checkout, or PostgreSQL connection admission.
Validate whether adding workers under this load prevents the job worker from acquiring a connection.

keyEvidence.description: Connection activity output lists active order history queries.
The query plan for the order history query shows a sequential scan on orders.
The application log shows SQLAlchemy QueuePool timeouts.
The application pool settings allow 10 pooled and 10 overflow connections per worker.

recommendedRecovery: Inspect pg_stat_activity to see connection use and the queries holding connections.
Run EXPLAIN on the order history query and identify the sequential scan.
Create the index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so writes continue.
Budget connections across all clients using worker concurrency and measured demand. Pool limits are upper bounds, not preallocated connections.
